title: HAD-Stack
subtitle: Physics as a referee in an adversarial game
context: Advisor: Prof. Aneesh S. Chivukula, BITS Pilani
paper: HAD-Stack: Hamiltonian Stackelberg Game for Robust Fraud Detection
status: Co-authored; under review at IEEE DSAA 2026.
headline: Fraudsters Adapt. So Should the Detector.
summary: Fraud detectors get attacked by people who learn their blind spots. Usually "how strong is the attacker?" is a number someone hand-picks. In HAD-Stack, the attacker and defender play a leader-follower (Stackelberg) game, and the knobs come from physics instead: one quantum-inspired Hamiltonian sets the attacker's budget, another sets how hard the defender regularizes, and a third decides when the game has settled into equilibrium.
result: 0.9948 clean AUC-ROC on 26,393 real UPI transactions, with false positives halved compared with a strong Transformer baseline (42 → 21), and still robust (AUC 0.9988) under an FGSM evasion attack.
note: Found and removed data leakage. Features that secretly encoded the label were inflating results, and they were removed before reporting.

title: Hamiltonian solvers, Bose–Hubbard dynamics & QHNet
subtitle: BITS Pilani study project (CS F266), Mar 2026
context: BITS Pilani study project (CS F266), Mar 2026, supervised by Prof. Chivukula
headline: Solving Physics That Depends on Its Own Answer
summary: Some quantum systems have a catch-22: the equation depends on its own solution. I built iterative "self-consistent" solvers that guess, solve, update, and repeat until the answer stops changing, for two-mode bosonic systems and a 4-qubit Pauli system. I also simulated the Bose–Hubbard model (bosons hopping on a 4-site lattice) with Trotterized time evolution, which conserved particle number and showed the expected superfluid oscillations. Finally, I built a graph neural network (QHNet) that learns Hamiltonian matrices from operator graphs while enforcing Hermiticity, so its outputs are physically valid.

title: Targeted attacks on an image classifier (MNIST)
subtitle: BITS Pilani study project, May 2026
headline: How to Make a 3 Look Like a 4
summary: Trained a CNN on handwritten digits, then attacked it with targeted Projected Gradient Descent: tiny, nearly invisible pixel changes that push the model toward a chosen wrong answer. Tracked attacker success and "regret" over rounds, which motivated the adaptive game design in HAD-Stack.
